title: Common Mistakes – Mixing Coordinate Systems
description: Lesson about why you cannot mix Cartesian and polar coordinates directly, and how to convert before combining sets.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Quick warning about a sneaky mistake I’ve seen pop up.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message:
Sometimes you’ll have a set in Cartesian coords, like 
A = {(x,y) ∣ x²+y² ≤ 1}.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: And another in polar coords, like B = {(r,θ) ∣ r=2, θ∈[0,2π)}.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message:
And some of you… try to take their intersection or union straight away. 
{(x,y) ∣ x²+y² ≤ 1} ∩ {(r,θ) ∣ r=2, θ∈[0,2π)}

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Bad idea! Why? Because (x,y) and (r,θ) are two totally different coordinate systems.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: It’s like trying to compare €5 with 120 CZK without converting first.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Before combining sets, always convert them into the same coordinate system.

factData.text2: Convert sets into the same notation before combining them
factData.speaker: Assistant

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Let’s practice. Convert A = {(x,y) ∣ x²+y² ≤ 1} into polar coordinates... let's start with radius r.

answers.feedback: Correct! The inequality x²+y² ≤ 1 becomes r² ≤ 1, so r ≤ 1.
Close — that’s only the boundary circle. We need the whole disc inside as well.
No, r ≥ 1 would describe everything outside the unit circle, not the disc.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Now, let’s do the angle θ.

answers.feedback: No, [0,π) would only give you half the circle — you’d miss the other half.
Correct! To cover the full disc, θ must go all the way around from 0 to 2π.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message:
Perfect! So we can write the same set in polar coords as:
{(r,θ) ∣ r ≤ 1, θ ∈ [0,2π)}.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Now let’s switch the other way around.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Convert B = {(r,θ) ∣ r=2, θ∈[0,2π)} into Cartesian coordinates:

answers.feedback: Check carefully: r is the radius itself, not squared.
No, r=2 describes the circle boundary, not the whole disc.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: And the equation in Cartesian coordinates is…

answers.feedback: No, r is 2, but we need radius²=4.
Not quite — the equation for a circle involves addition, not subtraction.
Correct! The circle of radius 2 has equation x²+y²=4.
Not quite — the equation for a circle involves addition, not subtraction.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Now the union can be written as: {(x,y) ∣ x²+y² ≤ 1} ∪ {(x,y) ∣ x²+y² = 4}.

imageData.description: Unit disc and circle of radius 2

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Great! So what was the main message of this lesson?

answers.text: Never mix sets from different coordinate systems until you convert them.
Polar coordinates are always better than Cartesian.
answers.feedback: Not quite — the important part is consistency, not preference.
